<reason>Both sides were sharp and the clash narrowed well, but CON built the stronger path. CON flipped PRO's calculator analogy (permission arrived after the skill was internalized; PRO's own "when arithmetic is the skill" exception covers nearly every pre-college essay), showed that oral defense—not disclosure—was PRO's real safeguard and works under either default, and gave an unrebutted mechanism for why the default matters (the plagiarism norm shaping the marginal student even under imperfect detection). Most decisively, CON exploited PRO's answer that the honest heavy user gets incomplete credit: if truthful heavy disclosure costs the grade, the honesty dividend collapses and the log is falsified, leaving only light users—who nobody restricts under either rule. PRO's closing reply (process users file because it is credit) only covers the light/genuine-process case, not CON's "middle zone" of outsourced thinking. PRO's "banned empty room is an A with no receipt" was memorable and its unenforceability point remained live, but PRO never addressed the overhead arithmetic or the norm argument. CON's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a real execution cost that keeps the margin competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 turn on PRO's A1: by conceding the disclosed heavy user earns incomplete credit, PRO made truthful disclosure self-incriminating, so the heavy user lies in the log just as under a ban—"the secrecy PRO promised to end returns, now with a form to falsify." PRO's closing only partially recovered by pointing to genuine process-users.</best_rebuttal>
